metadata.title: The digital divide in online education: Inequality in digital readiness of students and schools

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses secondary international large-scale survey data from ICILS 2018 (students and schools in 7 countries) and TALIS 2018 (teachers in 45 countries). The manuscript emphasizes representativeness requirements from IEA and OECD, but it does not report the application of complex survey weights or any specific weight variable names, nor does it mention replicate-weight procedures. For the ICILS student-level outcomes, the authors instead use clustered standard errors at the school level to account for nested structure, and for TALIS they fit multilevel models with teachers nested in schools, again without reporting explicit sampling-weight usage. Because no weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate schemes are documented, the weighting strategy cannot be verified from the text; analysts should consult the ICILS/TALIS data documentation to apply the appropriate design weights when producing population-representative estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports that missing values for the ICT-use factor scores are imputed using the row-mean of non-missing manifest variables, but it does not provide a complete, transparent missing-data strategy for all variables used in the regression models (e.g., whether listwise deletion was applied for other constructs, how missingness in SES/migration/gender indicators was handled, and whether any additional imputation was used). This is a reporting gap because ICILS/TALIS datasets typically contain non-trivial missingness across questionnaire items and derived scales, and the analysis relies on multiple constructed indicators (factor scores and standardized scales). As a result, the exact missing-data handling for the full analytic pipeline cannot be fully audited.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Study I uses ICILS 2018 data restricted to eighth-grade students in seven countries (Chile, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, South Korea) with available high-quality student- and school-level data; the analytic sample comprises N=18,882 students in 213 schools. The authors construct student ICT-use factor scores from 12 educational ICT-use manifest variables (excluding non-educational ICT-use items) and include only manifest variables with relatively few missing values and loadings ≥0.35; missing values for the factor scores are imputed using the row-mean of non-missing manifest variables as predictors. Student ICT skills are measured using a factor score based on the five plausible values from the ICILS Computer and Information Literacy Achievement scale. School ICT infrastructure and competencies are constructed from principals’/ICT coordinators’ evaluations using factor analysis on 40 manifest variables, again retaining only indicators with loadings ≥0.35. Study II uses TALIS 2018 teacher data restricted to teachers in lower-secondary schools in 45 countries; two countries are excluded due to missing data on teachers’ degree level (Spain) and the percentage of migrant students (United States).

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2018 Grade 8 (Computer and Information Literacy) — Student ICT use
main_findings.target_variable: Student ICT use for school-related activities (factor score)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (effects summarized as predicted differences in standard deviations; e.g., SES inequality up to 0.44 SD in Finland/Germany/Italy/Korea; migration differences ≤0.2 SD in Chile/France/Germany/Italy; girls up to 0.33 SD higher than boys in Korea).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018 Grade 8 the study leveraged socioeconomic status quartiles, migration background, and gender to predict students’ ICT use for school-related activities, finding that SES-related inequality is larger in Finland, Germany, Italy, and Korea (up to 0.44 SD) while migration-background and gender gaps are generally small (migration differences ≤0.2 SD; girls up to 0.33 SD higher than boys in Korea). This indicates that pre-pandemic digital readiness gaps in ICT use are present but are driven more by student skills/SES than by school-context differences, suggesting that early SES-targeted support for digital learning routines may be more urgent than broad school infrastructure interventions alone.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2018 Grade 8 (Computer and Information Literacy) — Student ICT skills
main_findings.target_variable: Student ICT skills (factor score from five plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (effects summarized as standard deviations; SES gaps up to 1.3 SD in Chile; Denmark highest vs lowest SES difference 0.48 SD; migration gaps up to 0.54 SD lower for migrants in several countries; gender gaps up to 0.44 SD higher for girls).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018 Grade 8 the study leveraged socioeconomic status quartiles, migration background, and gender to predict students’ ICT skills, finding that SES is the strongest driver of skill inequality (up to 1.3 SD between highest and lowest SES quartiles in Chile), with additional migration-background disadvantages (up to 0.54 SD lower for migrants in some countries) and a consistent girls’ advantage (up to 0.44 SD). This indicates that strengthening student digital skills—especially for low-SES and, where observed, migrant students—may be the most effective lever for reducing readiness gaps before online schooling is required again, though the study is correlational and does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (effects summarized as standard deviations; SES inequality only in Chile with high-SES students’ schools 0.59 SD above low-SES; migration inequality only in Finland with migrants’ schools 0.16 SD higher; no gender inequality).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018 Grade 8 the study leveraged student SES quartiles, migration background, and gender to predict schools’ ICT infrastructure, finding that school infrastructure varies substantially across countries but shows little stratification by student composition within countries (notably, SES inequality appears only in Chile at 0.59 SD; migration inequality only in Finland at 0.16 SD; and no gender-related infrastructure gaps). This indicates that compensatory school-level policies may have limited impact on infrastructure-based inequities in most countries, shifting attention toward student skill development as the primary source of the digital divide.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (effects summarized as standard deviations; no SES or gender gaps in any country; migration gap only in Finland where migrants’ schools are 0.33 SD better skilled).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018 Grade 8 the study leveraged student SES quartiles, migration background, and gender to predict schools’ ICT competencies, finding that these school-level competencies are largely unrelated to student composition (no SES or gender gaps across countries; migration gaps only in Finland at 0.33 SD). This indicates that, in the pre-pandemic baseline, schools do not systematically differ in ICT competencies in ways that track student disadvantage, implying that policy should prioritize within-student skill remediation rather than assuming that disadvantaged students are consistently placed in less digitally competent schools.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2018 Grade 8 — Overall digital readiness (combined indicator)
main_findings.target_variable: Overall digital readiness (average of standardized student and school indicators)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (effects summarized as standard deviations; SES inequality most pronounced in Chile at 0.84 SD and least in Denmark at 0.23 SD; migration gaps small with Denmark exception where migrants are disadvantaged by 0.19 SD; girls’ premium ranges from 0.31 SD in Korea to <0.1 SD in Chile/Italy).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018 Grade 8 the study leveraged student SES quartiles, migration background, and gender to predict overall multidimensional digital readiness, finding that students are best prepared in Denmark (followed by Finland and Korea) and least prepared in Germany and France, while SES inequality is substantial across countries (up to 0.84 SD in Chile) and girls are consistently better prepared (up to 0.31 SD in Korea). This indicates that reducing digital readiness gaps requires SES- and gender-sensitive interventions at the student level, while migration-related disadvantages are more context-specific and may require targeted support rather than uniform measures.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 Lower-secondary teachers (ICT readiness indicators) — ICT in teacher education
main_findings.target_variable: ICT in teacher education and training (standardized continuous scale)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (effects summarized as standard deviations; significant negative relationship with low-SES and migration shares occurs only in Mexico: teachers 0.2 SD and 0.12 SD less well trained, respectively; Lithuania shows positive low-SES effect at 0.28 SD for >60% disadvantaged schools).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 lower-secondary teacher the study leveraged school composition measures for low-SES and migrant shares (plus teacher characteristics) to predict teachers’ ICT attention in teacher education, finding that significant relationships are rare and inconsistent across countries (e.g., Mexico shows negative associations of 0.2 SD and 0.12 SD, while Lithuania shows a positive 0.28 SD for high low-SES schools). This indicates that school-level teacher training in ICT is not systematically stratified by student disadvantage, suggesting that broad teacher-training equity policies may need to be targeted to specific contexts rather than assumed to automatically align with student composition.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 Lower-secondary teachers — ICT during professional development
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (effects summarized as percentage-point differences; England: >60% low-SES schools are 24 percentage points less likely to have attended ICT-related professional development; Norway: >60% disadvantaged schools are 28 percentage points more likely).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 lower-secondary teacher the study leveraged school composition measures for low-SES and migrant shares (plus teacher characteristics) to predict whether teachers’ professional development included ICT, finding that most countries show no statistically significant relationship and that exceptions are directionally mixed (e.g., England: −24 percentage points for high low-SES schools; Norway: +28 percentage points). This indicates that teacher ICT professionalization is not consistently patterned by student disadvantage, so equity-oriented interventions may require monitoring and targeted resource allocation rather than relying on school composition as a proxy.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 Lower-secondary teachers — ICT for classwork
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (effects summarized as standard deviations; Australia: >60% low-SES schools show teachers letting students use ICT for classwork 0.6 SD less frequently; Italy: >60% migrant-background schools show 0.56 SD less frequent ICT use in class; positive SES-related effects not found; positive migrant-background association found in UAE and Estonia).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 lower-secondary teacher the study leveraged school composition measures for low-SES and migrant shares (plus teacher characteristics) to predict teachers’ ICT use for classwork, finding that significant relationships are more common but still not uniformly positive for disadvantaged groups (e.g., Australia shows −0.6 SD for high low-SES schools; Italy shows −0.56 SD for high migrant-background schools; no country shows a significant positive SES relationship). This indicates that, where teacher ICT use is stratified, it can disadvantage students in high-disadvantage schools, implying that targeted support for ICT integration in teaching may be needed in specific national contexts.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 Lower-secondary teachers — ICT for student support
main_findings.target_variable: ICT to support student learning (standardized categorical indicator)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (effects summarized as standard deviations; Singapore: >60% low-SES schools show teachers 0.36 SD less able to support students via ICT; for migration background, Singapore shows +0.28 SD for high migrant-background schools; most countries show insignificant relationships).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 lower-secondary teacher the study leveraged school composition measures for low-SES and migrant shares (plus teacher characteristics) to predict teachers’ ICT use to support student learning, finding that relationships are mostly insignificant but can be directionally mixed across countries (e.g., Singapore shows −0.36 SD for high low-SES schools and +0.28 SD for high migrant-background schools). This indicates that compensatory teacher ICT practices are not consistently aligned with student disadvantage, so policy should emphasize context-specific diagnosis and targeted professional support rather than assuming uniform school-level compensation.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses ICILS 2018 (grade 8) and TALIS 2018 to examine pre-pandemic digital readiness gaps across seven and 45 countries, respectively. In ICILS, the authors construct student ICT-use factor scores and ICT-skill factor scores (from five plausible values) and school ICT infrastructure/competencies from principal/ICT coordinator evaluations, then estimate linear regression models with school-clustered standard errors. The results show that digital readiness inequalities are strongest for students’ ICT skills and are most pronounced by SES (up to 1.3 SD in Chile), with additional migration and gender patterns (e.g., migrants up to 0.54 SD lower in skills in some countries; girls up to 0.44 SD higher). In TALIS, multilevel country-specific models indicate that school composition has very weak explanatory power for teachers’ ICT readiness, with only sporadic significant relationships (e.g., England −24 percentage points; Norway +28 percentage points for ICT professional development). The paper does not report ML model performance metrics because it uses regression-based approaches rather than predictive ML, and it does not document a complete missing-data strategy beyond row-mean imputation for one factor score, limiting full transparency.
